steps.label: Composition
lines: The middle lamella is the thin layer lying
between the walls of two neighbouring cells.
It is made mainly of calcium pectate, with
steps.why: The question names two parts. The first is answered by the pectate salts, which are sticky and hold the two walls together.
common_mistakes: Writing cellulose. Cellulose builds the primary and secondary wall, not the middle lamella.
Writing calcium pectin. The salt is calcium pectate.
steps.memory_tip: Middle lamella = the layer between two walls, made of calcium pectate.
steps.margin_note: Both salts named earns this mark.

steps.label: Significance
lines: It sticks the two adjacent cells firmly
together, so groups of cells stay joined and
When it dissolves, as in a ripening fruit,
the cells separate and the fruit softens.
steps.why: One layer of sticky pectate between every pair of cells is what turns separate cells into a tissue — and when it breaks down, the tissue falls apart.
common_mistakes: Writing that the middle lamella gives strength to the wall. That is cellulose; the middle lamella joins cells.
Leaving out tissue formation, which is the second half of the question.
steps.memory_tip: Dissolve the middle lamella and the cells come apart — that is why ripe fruit is soft.

insider_note: Two questions in one line, so write two separate sentences — one on composition, one on the joining function.
